title: Prompt caching
summary: Prompt caching lets a request resume from a prefix the API has already processed, so repeated content is cheaper and faster. You mark where the reusable prefix ends with `cache_control`, and the cache lives 5 minutes by default.
keyPoints: Cache reads cost a small fraction of base input (**0.1×** on most models, lower on some newer ones); 5-minute writes cost 1.25×, 1-hour writes 2×.
The prefix is built in order: `tools` → `system` → `messages`, up to and including the `cache_control` block.
Put static content first and the breakpoint on the **last identical block**, never on content that varies.
Default lifetime is **5 minutes**, refreshed at no cost on every hit; `"ttl": "1h"` extends it.
Up to **4** breakpoints; each model has a minimum cacheable prompt length.

sections.heading: What caching buys you
sections.body:
When a request starts with the same content as a recent one, the API can resume from that cached prefix instead of processing it again. This significantly reduces processing time and cost for prompts with consistent elements, and long documents generally see better time-to-first-token.

Pricing is relative to the base input price:

- Cache read: 0.1× on most models (lower on some newer ones, e.g. 0.05× on Claude Opus 5.5)
- 5-minute cache write: 1.25×
- 1-hour cache write: 2×

diagram.caption: A cached prefix is billed at the read rate; only the new part costs full price.

sections.heading: Placing the breakpoint
sections.body:
Caching covers the whole prompt (`tools`, `system`, then `messages`) up to and including the block marked with `cache_control`. Place static content such as tool definitions, instructions and examples at the beginning.

Put `cache_control` on the last block whose prefix is identical across the requests you want to share a cache. If the prompt ends with something that varies (a timestamp, per-request context, the incoming message), put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix, not on the varying block.

Changes at one level invalidate that level and everything after it, so editing a tool definition invalidates the cached system prompt and messages too.

sections.heading: Lifetime and limits
sections.body:
By default the cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed at no extra cost each time the cached content is used. If traffic has longer gaps, set `"ttl": "1h"` on `cache_control` for the 1-hour duration, at a higher write price.

You can define up to 4 breakpoints, for example to cache sections that change at different rates. Prompts shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length are not cached.

sections.heading: Counting tokens before you send
sections.body:
The token counting endpoint (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`) takes the same inputs as a Messages request and returns an estimate of the total input tokens. It is free to use, with its own requests-per-minute limits.

Token counting doesn't use caching logic: you can include `cache_control` blocks, but prompt caching only happens when a message is actually created. Count under the model you plan to use, because Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text.

title: LLM fundamentals
summary: A language model reads and writes tokens, and everything it works with at once must fit in its context window, the model's "working memory". Temperature controls how random the output is, and even at temperature 0 the API isn't fully deterministic. Examples in the prompt (few-shot) are one of the most reliable ways to steer it.
keyPoints: The glossary's **rough** ratio is about 3.5 English characters per token; Claude 4.7 and later tokenizers produce about **30% more** tokens, so count real prompts.
The context window includes the **response itself**; system prompt, messages, tools and thinking all count, and cached prefixes still count.
More context isn't automatically better: accuracy and recall degrade as tokens grow (**context rot**).
Even with **temperature 0**, identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls.
Few-shot examples should be relevant, diverse and in `<example>` tags; **3–5** work best.

sections.heading: Tokens and next-token prediction
sections.body:
Tokens are the smallest units a language model works in. They can be words, subwords, characters or even bytes. Anthropic's glossary puts a Claude token at approximately 3.5 English characters, though the exact number varies by language. Treat that as a rough ratio: Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text, so get real counts from the token counting API for the model you plan to use.

In pretraining, autoregressive models like Claude's underlying model are trained on a large unlabeled corpus to predict the next word from the previous context. Pretrained models are not inherently good at answering questions or following instructions. Fine-tuning and RLHF refine them, and Claude has already been fine-tuned to be a helpful assistant.

sections.heading: The context window
sections.body:
The context window is all the text a model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself. It is a working memory, separate from the training data.

Everything in a request counts: the system prompt, every message (tool results, images and documents too), tool definitions, and the output, including thinking. Cached prefixes still occupy the window; caching changes what you pay, not whether they count.

- Input alone over the window: 400 "prompt is too long", on every model
- Input plus `max_tokens` over the window, on Claude 4.5 models and newer: accepted, and it may stop with `model_context_window_exceeded`
- More tokens can mean worse accuracy and recall (context rot), so curate what goes in

diagram.caption: Everything in the request, plus the output, shares one window.

sections.heading: Temperature and non-determinism
sections.body:
Temperature controls the randomness of a model's predictions. Higher temperatures give more creative and diverse outputs; lower temperatures give more conservative, deterministic outputs that stick to the most probable phrasing.

Even with temperature set to 0, results are not fully deterministic: identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls. This is true of Anthropic's own service and of third-party cloud providers.

sections.heading: Steering with examples (few-shot)
sections.body:
A few well-crafted examples, known as few-shot or multishot prompting, improve accuracy and consistency. Make them:

- Relevant: mirror your actual use case closely
- Diverse: cover edge cases, so Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns
- Structured: wrap each in `<example>` tags, and a set in `<examples>`

Include 3–5 examples for best results.

title: Calling the Claude API
summary: The Claude API is a RESTful API at `https://api.anthropic.com`. Requests need an API key or access token, an `anthropic-version` header and a JSON content type, and the official SDKs send these for you and add retries. Set `"stream": true` to get the reply as server-sent events, and handle each event type in order.
keyPoints: Required headers: auth (`Authorization: Bearer` or legacy `x-api-key`), `anthropic-version` and `content-type: application/json`.
Official client SDKs: **Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby**.
SDKs retry connection errors, rate limits and 5xx errors **twice by default**, with backoff; configure with `max_retries`.
Stream order: `message_start` → content blocks (start, deltas, stop) → `message_delta` → `message_stop`.
Messages requests are capped at **32 MB**; over that is a 413 `request_too_large`.

sections.heading: Requests and headers
sections.body:
The Messages API is `POST /v1/messages`. Every request includes:

- `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (or `x-api-key`, a legacy fallback that is still supported)
- `anthropic-version`, for example `2023-06-01`
- `content-type: application/json`

`anthropic-workspace-id` is also required with a multi-workspace API key. Requests have size limits: 32 MB for Messages and Token Counting, 256 MB for Message Batches and 500 MB for the Files API. Going over returns a 413 `request_too_large` error.

sections.heading: The SDKs
sections.body:
Anthropic's client SDKs for Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby manage headers automatically and provide type safety and built-in streaming, retries and error handling. The Claude Agent SDK is different: it works at a higher level, providing the agent loop and tool execution.

The SDKs automatically retry transient failures (connection errors, rate limits and 5xx server errors) with exponential backoff, twice by default, and honor `retry-after` when it is present. Use `max_retries` (TypeScript, Java, PHP: `maxRetries`) to configure or disable this.

sections.heading: Streaming over server-sent events
sections.body:
With `"stream": true`, the response arrives as server-sent events. `message_start` carries a `Message` with empty `content`. Each content block then has a `content_block_start`, one or more `content_block_delta` events and a `content_block_stop`. One or more `message_delta` events follow, whose `usage` counts are cumulative, and `message_stop` ends the stream.

- `ping` events can appear anywhere
- New event types may be added, so handle unknown ones gracefully
- Tool input streams as `input_json_delta` partial JSON: accumulate it, then parse at `content_block_stop`
- Errors can arrive mid-stream after a 200, for example `overloaded_error`

For large `max_tokens` values the SDKs require streaming to avoid HTTP timeouts. If you only need the finished reply, `.get_final_message()` (Python) or `.finalMessage()` (TypeScript) returns the complete `Message`.

title: Choosing a model and effort
summary: Choosing a Claude model means balancing capability, speed and cost. Start most workloads on Claude Opus 5.5; use Claude Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when evals on Opus 5.5 at higher effort still fall short. Within one model, the effort parameter is often a better lever than switching models.
keyPoints: **Fable 5.1** $10/$50, slower · **Opus 5.5** $4/$20, moderate · **Sonnet 5** $2/$10, fast · **Haiku 4.5** $1/$5, fastest (per input/output MTok).
If unsure, start with **Claude Opus 5.5**; move to **Fable 5.1** when evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short.
Effort runs `low` → `max`; default `high` on most models, `medium` on Claude Opus 5.5. Lower effort cuts latency and cost.
Manual `budget_tokens`: at least **1,024** and below `max_tokens`; above 32k use batch processing. Claude 4.7 and later reject it.

sections.heading: The current lineup
sections.body:
- Claude Fable 5.1: demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Slower latency; $10 / $50 per input / output MTok
- Claude Opus 5.5: long-running agentic coding and knowledge work. Moderate latency; $4 / $20
- Claude Sonnet 5: the best combination of speed and intelligence. Fast; $2 / $10
- Claude Haiku 4.5: the fastest model, with near-frontier intelligence. Fastest; $1 / $5

Batch API requests are 50% off. Actual latency depends on prompt length, output length and thinking effort.

sections.heading: Two starting strategies
sections.body:
Efficiency-first starts with Claude Haiku 4.5 and upgrades only for specific capability gaps. It suits prototyping, tight latency, cost-sensitive and high-volume straightforward tasks.

Capability-first starts with Claude Opus 5.5, then optimizes down by lowering effort or switching models. It suits complex reasoning and cases where accuracy outweighs cost. If evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work, move to Claude Fable 5.1.

Either way, build an evaluation set from your real prompts and data: the guide calls this the most important step.

diagram.caption: The capability-first path in the model guide.

sections.heading: Effort and thinking
sections.body:
Effort (`output_config.effort`) controls how many tokens Claude spends, across text, tool calls and thinking. Levels run `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. Lower effort gives token savings with some capability reduction; `low` suits simple, speed-sensitive tasks such as subagents. On Claude Opus 5.5 adaptive thinking is always on, and `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` returns a 400 error.

On models that support only manual extended thinking (such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5), `budget_tokens` sets the thinking target: at least 1,024 and less than `max_tokens`. Larger budgets can improve quality, with diminishing returns and more latency. Above 32k, use batch processing to avoid timeouts. Claude 4.7 and later models reject `budget_tokens` with a 400.
